The controls might\\\\nnot be available in all AWS Regions. For more information, see Availability of controls by Region\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/securityhub/latest/userguide/bedrock-controls.html\"},{\"rank_order\":2,\"title\":\"Automated network incident response with AWS DevOps Agent | Networking & Content Delivery\",\"context\":\"## Scenario 4: Bedrock Interface Endpoint subnets removed, AI feature breaks\\\\n\\\\nThe Bedrock Runtime Interface Endpoint (`simulated-workload-Bedrock-Endpoint`) creates ENIs in two private subnets. Private DNS resolves `bedrock-runtime.us-east-1.amazonaws.com` to those ENI IP addresses. The following Figure 21 shows the removal of subnet association.\\\\n\\\\n*[](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/5b384ce32d8cdef02bc3a139d4cac0a22bb029e8/2026/04/17/NetCDNBlog-1723-image-21.gif)Figure 21: Modify subnets associated with interface VPC endpoint*\\\\n\\\\nWhen someone removes both subnet associations, the ENIs are deleted. The endpoint still exists and Private DNS still resolves the hostname to the endpoint, but there is nothing to handle the traffic. This is the scenario that is particularly hard to spot by hand, because the console still shows the endpoint as \u201cAvailable\u201d even though requests time out with no response. It is worth noting the difference between the two endpoint types: VPC Gateway Endpoints (Amazon S3, Amazon DynamoDB) work through route table entries and endpoint policies, so a misconfiguration there returns an Access Denied (HTTP 403 Forbidden) error. Interface VPC Endpoints (Amazon Bedrock and many other AWS services) work through ENIs in your subnets with their own security groups, so when those ENIs are gone, you get connection timeouts instead. But the database still works (VPC local route), Amazon S3 still works (VPC Gateway Endpoint has its own route table entry), and outbound internet connectivity still works (NAT Gateway route is intact). Only the Bedrock AI check turns red.\\\\n\\\\n[](https://d2908q01vomqb2.cloudfront.net/5b384ce32d8cdef02bc3a139d4cac0a22bb029e8/2026/04/17/NetCDNBlog-1723-image-22.png)*Figure 22: Simulated workload application status page*\\\\n\\\\nDevOps Agent receives the `BedrockAccessFailures` alarm and investigates:\\\\n\\\\n1. **Checks endpoint configuration** \u2013 Finds zero subnet associations on the Interface VPC Endpoint.\\\\n2. **Searches CloudTrail logs** \u2013 Finds the `ModifyVpcEndpoint` API call, including who removed the subnet associations\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/networking-and-content-delivery/automated-network-incident-response-with-aws-devops-agent/\"},{\"rank_order\":3,\"title\":\"Integrating a traditional cloud workload with Amazon Bedrock\",\"context\":\"### Network security\\\\n\\\\nDeploy your application within a virtual private cloud (VPC) by using private subnets for application tiers that don\\'t require direct internet access. Use VPC endpoints to establish private connectivity to Amazon Bedrock services, to help make sure traffic between your application and Amazon Bedrock doesn\\'t traverse the public internet.\\\\n\\\\nConfigure security groups with restrictive rules that allow only necessary traffic between application tiers. Implement network access control lists (network ACLs) as an additional defensive layer with explicit allow rules for required traffic and a default-deny posture. Deploy AWS Network Firewall for deep packet inspection of traffic between application tiers and to detect unusual request patterns that might indicate attacks\",\"url\":\"https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/security-reference-architecture-generative-ai/bedrock-integration.html\"},{\"rank_order\":4,\"title\":\"Use AWS PrivateLink to set up private access to Amazon Bedrock | Artificial Intelligence\",\"context\":\"## Test private access controls\\\\n\\\\nNow you can test the private access controls (Amazon Bedrock APIs over VPC endpoints).\\\\n\\\\n1. Return to the Lambda function page and on the **Code** tab, choose **Test**.\\\\n\\\\nAs shown in the following screenshot, the access request to Amazon Bedrock over the VPC endpoint was denied (Status: Failed).\\\\n\\\\nThrough this testing process, we demonstrated how traffic from your VPC to the Amazon Bedrock API endpoint is traversing over the PrivateLink connection and not through the internet connection\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/use-aws-privatelink-to-set-up-private-access-to-amazon-bedrock/\"},{\"rank_order\":5,\"title\":\"Considerations for addressing the core dimensions of responsible AI for Amazon Bedrock applications | Artificial Intelligence\",\"context\":\"### Built-in security and privacy of Amazon Bedrock\\\\n\\\\nWith Amazon Bedrock, if we look from a data privacy and localization perspective, AWS does not store your data\u2014if we don\u2019t store it, it can\u2019t leak, it can\u2019t be seen by model vendors, and it can\u2019t be used by AWS for any other purpose. The only data we store is operational metrics\u2014for example, for accurate billing, AWS collects metrics on how many tokens you send to a specific Amazon Bedrock model and how many tokens you receive in a model output. And, of course, if you create a fine-tuned model, we need to store that in order for AWS to host it for you. Data used in your API requests remains in the AWS Region of your choosing\u2014API requests to the Amazon Bedrock API to a specific Region will remain completely within that Region.\\\\n\\\\nIf we look at data security, a common adage is that if it moves, encrypt it. Communications to, from, and within Amazon Bedrock are encrypted in transit\u2014Amazon Bedrock doesn\u2019t have a non-TLS endpoint. Another adage is that if it doesn\u2019t move, encrypt it. Your fine-tuning data and model will by default be encrypted using AWS managed AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) keys, but you have the option to use your own KMS keys.\\\\n\\\\nWhen it comes to identity and access management, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) controls who is authorized to use Amazon Bedrock resources. For each model, you can explicitly allow or deny access to actions. For example, one team or account could be allowed to provision capacity for Amazon Titan Text, but not Anthropic models. You can be as broad or as granular as you need to be.\\\\n\\\\nLooking at network data flows for Amazon Bedrock API access, it\u2019s important to remember that traffic is encrypted at all time. If you\u2019re using Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC), you can use AWS PrivateLink to provide your VPC with private connectivity through the regional network direct to the frontend fleet of Amazon Bedrock, mitigating exposure of your VPC to internet traffic with an internet gateway. Similarly, from a corporate data center perspective, you can set up a VPN or AWS Direct Connect connection to privately connect to a VPC, and from there you can have that traffic sent to Amazon Bedrock over PrivateLink. This should negate the need for your on-premises systems to send Amazon Bedrock related traffic over the\\\\n\\\\n*[truncated \u2014 additional content omitted]*\",\"url\":\"https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/machine-learning/considerations-for-addressing-the-core-dimensions-of-responsible-ai-for-amazon-bedrock-applications/\"}]}}\\n\\n## Recent AWS announcements (What\\'s New)\\n\\nNewer than your training data may be. When these conflict with the documentation results above or with what you remember, prefer the most recent dated source.\\n\\n{\"content\":{\"result\":[{\"rank_order\":1,\"title\":\"AWS Security Hub CSPM launches AI Security Best Practices standard with 31 automated controls - AWS\",\"context\":\"AWS Security Hub CSPM has introduced the AI Security Best Practices standard, which includes 31 automated security controls for detecting misalignments between security best practices and deployed AI resources. These controls cover critical security domains such as network isolation, encryption, VPC placement, KMS key usage, private container registry requirements, and authorization controls. The standard applies to various components of AI infrastructure, including Bedrock AgentCore runtimes, gateways, memory stores, custom browsers, SageMaker notebook instances, endpoints, models, monitoring jobs, and feature groups. The standard is available in all AWS Regions where Security Hub CSPM is available and can be accessed using the identifier \\\\\"standards/ai-security-best-practices/v/1.0.0\\\\\". Security teams can quickly identify and remediate misconfigurations using findings generated by each control, which is assigned a security category.
